quote: My my me and my wife was. But since my wife passed, I put my daughter on my insurance.
stewart_read: The customer discloses his wife's death unprompted while answering a routine title-ownership question. The rep's next line is a flat pivot to the credit-score qualifier with no acknowledgment of the loss.
alternative_hypothesis: Could be read as the rep respecting the customer's brevity and not dwelling, but the complete absence of any acknowledgment (not even 'I'm sorry to hear that') suggests a miss rather than a deliberate light touch.
coaching_implication: Coach a one-line acknowledgment ('I'm sorry for your loss') before moving to the next verify item — costs 3 seconds, protects rapport, and is the schema's explicit guidance for vulnerability disclosures.

quote: I have no idea what my score is or nothing.
stewart_read: Customer can't confirm the 670 credit threshold. Rep pivots to an informal proxy question ('Do you, like, pay your bills on time') rather than either hard-gating or explicitly deferring the decision to the closer's credit pull.
alternative_hypothesis: This could be read as smart schema-aware handling — since Spencer's operator note flags stated-credit unreliability, softening to a bill-payment proxy avoids a false DQ. But the rep never explicitly tells the customer 'the specialist will verify this properly,' so the qualifier is left unresolved rather than intentionally deferred.
coaching_implication: Flag this as an open policy question per qualifiers.credit_qualifier.policy_question_for_kenny — until Kenny resolves stated-vs-pulled credit, this rep's soft workaround (paying-bills-on-time proxy) is a reasonable improvisation, but it should be made explicit: 'No problem, the specialist will run an official check at your appointment.'

quote: Well, maybe you call later on when one of my grandchildren here, they can, assist you or whatever because I don't know nothing about this.
stewart_read: This is the near-exit point after roughly 8-9 minutes of failed texting. The schema's time budget for pivoting to verbal read-back is 2 minutes from first friction (first friction visible around 10:01 when customer says 'I don't know how to do that'); the rep didn't pivot to read-back until 15:04, well past budget.
alternative_hypothesis: The rep could be seen as reasonably trying every available channel (text, then email) before falling back to the more labor-intensive read-aloud method, which does work eventually. But the schema explicitly calls this out as a known failure mode from other calls (SESSION6, SESSION14 cited directly in schema), so the late pivot is a documented gap, not a novel judgment call.
coaching_implication: Coach recognition speed: when a customer says 'I don't know how to do that' on a smartphone task, that is the trigger to immediately offer verbal read-back, not to try a second digital channel (email) first.

quote: And how much it cost and all that?
stewart_read: Customer asks directly about cost. The rep's response ('Yeah. Exactly.') neither answers nor redirects using the schema's escape hatch — it's a non-answer that glosses past a scope-relevant question rather than bridging to the specialist.
alternative_hypothesis: The rep may have intentionally not engaged because the appointment was already being booked, treating the cost question as rhetorical throat-clearing rather than a real ask. But the schema's universal escape hatch line ('that's exactly what the specialist will walk you through') would have been a clean, low-cost way to both validate the question and protect appointment value.
coaching_implication: Coach the escape-hatch phrase for cost questions — even a vague or mumbled customer question about cost is the moment to plant 'the specialist will show you exact numbers Monday,' which also builds anticipation for the appointment.
